Nah there's a thing called a hydra (yeah hail hydra meme, whatever), that basically get's old and instead of dying reverts back to a previous part of it's lifecycle. Like a spawn hatching into a tadpole that grows into a frog, ages and then settles down and over the course of a few hours regrows it's tail and loses it's legs and shrinks to tadpole size to continue living.

The actually interesting part of that outside the whole "I'm a teenager again!" thing is that they actually regenerate their telomerase in their cells. That's the stuff that get's cut a little shorter every time a cell divides, so your cells don't just split forever and you end up with cancers all over you all the time, you still get cancer when something mutates and breaks that mechanic though. So they basically truly become young again, not just change shape.

That's pretty amazing from a biology perspective, we don't know how they do it but if we did we'd have like two corner pieces and a patch of sky in the great puzzle of immortality. If we could regenerate the telomerase in our cells, and not cause explosive cancer proliferation in doing so (it would basically make a human look like a mushroom after a few days, a mushroom of pain), then we could truly live forever in the prime of our life. There would be some unknowns, like some brain cells that don't divide and what happens to those beyond a human lifetime, but it would be pretty much immortality.

Very different animals -- they're even different at the "order" level. Parrots have more genetic diversity and eat a more vegetable-based diet. Eagles eat meat and live in restricted areas.

Interestingly, the typical age of an animal before dying of old age is inversely proportional to its typical heart rate. Small animals tend to have higher heart than larger ones, and warm blooded higher than cold blooded ones, and correspondingly have shorter lifespans. All animals have a lifetime of about one billion heart beats. The big exception to this are humans, who tend to get over two billion.
